Confound
kon-FOWND
v.
Latin confundere: con- (together) + fundere (to pour)—to pour together, to mix into disorder. From the mixing sense comes the second: to be thrown into disorder is to be put to shame, and the KJV uses both.

Biblical Definition

Confound carries two joined senses in the KJV: to mix into confusion, and to put to shame. The first is Babel, where God says, let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech (Gen 11:7)—a judgment executed by mixing, the one unified rebel project broken by making speech unintelligible. The Hebrew wordplay is deliberate: the place is called Babel because there the LORD confounded the language. Pentecost is the deliberate reversal, where men of every tongue hear the wonderful works of God in their own language, and the multitude is again confounded, this time by grace rather than judgment. The shame sense runs through the prophets and the Psalms: let me never be confounded is the repeated prayer of the man who has trusted God publicly and would be humiliated if God failed. Peter applies it to Christ: he that believeth on him shall not be confounded (1 Pet 2:6). Paul then makes confounding an instrument of the gospel's strategy: God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty (1 Cor 1:27). And the whole is bounded by a rule about God's own character: God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints (1 Cor 14:33). God confounds rebels; He does not run His church that way.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CONFOUND as to mingle and blend so that things cannot be distinguished; to throw into disorder; to perplex; and to abash or put to shame.

expand to see more

CONFOUND, v.t. — To mingle and blend different things, so that their forms or natures cannot be distinguished; to mix in a mass or crowd, so that individuals cannot be discerned.

CONFOUND, v.t. — To perplex; to disconcert; to abash; to throw the mind into disorder. Hence, to put to shame. He that believeth on him shall not be confounded (1 Pet 2:6).

Key Scripture

Genesis 11:7 — "Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech."

1 Corinthians 1:27 — "But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;"

1 Corinthians 14:33 — "For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints."

1 Peter 2:6 — "Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded."

Modern Corruption

Confusion has been promoted from a judgment to a virtue—ambiguity as sophistication, the blurring of categories as progress—while confounded as public shame has faded, taking with it the force of the promise that the believer shall never be put to shame.

expand to see more

The Babel sense is worth holding onto because the modern instinct is to treat category confusion as maturity. Clear distinctions—between male and female, between the church and the world, between truth and preference—are described as simplistic, and the mixing of them as nuance. Genesis 11 says confounding was God's judicial act against a project of unified rebellion, and 1 Corinthians 14:33 says God is not the author of confusion in His churches. A church that cultivates ambiguity as its house style is imitating the judgment rather than the peace.

The shame sense has quietly disappeared, and its loss costs the believer a promise. To be confounded in Scripture is to have publicly trusted and been publicly humiliated—the terror behind let me never be confounded. Peter's assurance that the one who believes on Christ shall not be confounded is therefore not a statement about feelings but about the last day: the man who staked everything on this cornerstone will not be exposed as a fool. Modern confounded means merely puzzled, which reduces a promise about vindication to a remark about confusion.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew balal, to mix or confuse, the Babel verb, and bosh, to be ashamed; Greek kataischynō, to put to shame or disgrace.

expand to see more

Hebrew balal (H1101) — to mix, mingle, confuse; the verb behind the name Babel (Gen 11:7, 9).

Hebrew bosh (H954) — to be ashamed, disappointed, put to confusion; the psalmist's let me never be put to confusion (Ps 22:5; 31:1; 71:1; Isa 45:17).

Greek kataischynō (G2617) — to dishonor, put to shame, disgrace; used of God confounding the wise and of the believer never being confounded (Rom 5:5; 9:33; 1 Cor 1:27; 1 Pet 2:6).

Usage

"There confound their language—Babel: confusion as a judicial act of God."

"God is not the author of confusion, but of peace—the rule for His churches."

"He that believeth on him shall not be confounded—a promise of vindication, not of clarity."
